title.narrative: Improving Safe Access to Education Facilities in Syrian Cities

description.narrative: The COVID-19 pandemic has had a severe impact on the Syrian Arab Republic, especially following a 10-year protracted crisis which caused significant damage in rural and urban areas across the country and resulted in a decline in the functionality of basic services as well as a dramatic economic downturn. COVID-19 pandemic spread has significantly increased the vulnerability of the population. Syria registered its first case of COVID-19 on 22 March 2020. The Ministry of Health (MoH) reported 608 COVID-19 confirmed cases as of 24 July with 35 fatalities and 184 recovered. Although containment and social distancing measures were applied in Syria in March to limit the spread of the virus, it is important to note that the number of cases in July almost doubled the number in June . By 23 December, 10,442 laboratory-confirmed cases had been reported by the MoH . By 29 of December, the total number of infections registered in Syria was 112,43 . According to UN reports, the MoH reported that the increase in COVID-19 cases in Syria has overwhelmed the capacity of local hospitals. The repercussions of the conflict in Syria (damage to infrastructure, health, educational, other service institutions and housing, rapid and dynamic demographic change, economic factors aggravated Syrians’ socio-economic situation), as well as the spread of COVID-19, have increased the vulnerability of large segments of the Syrian population, especially in the densely populated areas hosting Internally Displaced People (IDPs) or witnessed returnees movement. The above-mentioned factors have affected and contributed to limit the capacities of municipalities/local authorities (materialistic and human resources gaps) from providing sustainable basic services (WASH, safe water supply, solid waste removal and management, debris removal, hygiene materials and adequate supply of personal protective equipment for cleaning workers) and responding to increased humanitarian needs of population, especially in areas which suffered from large scale damage and areas suffering from increased pressure on basic services and facilities due to hosting IDPs and increased number of returnees.
